sweep_summary: Khalaj (turk1303) is not in the catalog. The single title-works with stress in the title, Doerfer 1981 'Zur Betonung der Wortverbindungen des Chaladsch' (Scholia = Gabain Festschrift, Veröffentlichungen der Societas Uralo-Altaica 14, pp. 47-54, Harrassowitz; pages confirmed from the DNB ToC scan), is squarely about Khalaj word and phrase stress; no open copy exists (print-only; archive.org 0 hits, Google Books no-preview, HathiTrust/books.google page views blocked), but 18 verbatim Google Books full-text snippets were harvested and saved: word stress is on the last syllable ('normale Betonung'), a falling pitch always sits on the last syllable, exceptions start with Iranian loans (bä'li 'yes', xä'yli 'very'), and phrase stress (subject main / predicate secondary, level stress in coordination) is fixed by grammatical relation. The best first-hand statement read is Doerfer 1988 Grammatik des Chaladsch §3.4 p. 39 (snippets): default final stress with a closed list of unstressed suffixes (imperative, 1pl aorist, negative, copula, present predicate, -in, Persian izafat/indefinite) and vocative retraction to the first syllable; corroborated by the fully open Doerfer 1978 Belleten p. 23 ('Stress is just as in the other Turkic languages.. havda' : ha'vča'), Doerfer 1971 FUF 39 (imperative stem stress vs perfect suffix stress) and Ščerbak 1997 p. 472. Recommended new catalog's classification: fixed final stress, Turkic type, with morphological exceptions. Acquisition priority high for the print texts of Doerfer 1981 and Doerfer 1988 p. 39 to replace snippet reads with page reads.

(2) Exceptions are: a) some Persian words such as ba'li 'yes'; unstressed are the Persian suffixes -i (izafat) and -i (indefinite article ...) [...] the imperative (person) suffixes (a'l:dum 'I want to take' vs. al:du'm 'I took'); f) the 1st person plural of the aorist (hat:i'miz 'we throw' vs. hatimi'z 'our horse'); g) the negative suffix (a'l-ma 'don't take!'); h) the copular ('esse') suffixes (xala'c+am 'I am a Khalaj' ...); i) the predicate suffixes of the present; j) the verbal suffix -in. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the word (stem plus stressable suffixes), as in most Turkic languages; a closed set of suffixes/enclitics is unstressable so that stress stays on the syllable before them (negative -mA, copular and present-tense personal predicate endings, 1pl aorist person marker, non-2sg imperative person endings, -in, Persian izafat -i and indefinite -i), some Persian loans keep non-final stress, vocatives take initial stress, and emphasis can shift or level the stress. Doerfer 1978: 23 puts the same rule as 'Stress is just as in the other Turkic languages (or as in most of them), even in such cases as hàvdá : hávčà' (ablative stressed, locative -ča pre-stressing).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No rhythmic secondary stress rule recovered. Doerfer 1988 (5): in word groups 'entscheidet die grammatische Natur der Wörter über den Akzent, nämlich über die Distribution von Haupt- und Nebenakzent' (päsänd yetmä'k 'mögen' vs. päsä'nd yeti 'möge!'); Doerfer 1978 writes a grave (weaker) accent on the initial syllable opposite the main accent (hàvdá, hávčà); Doerfer 1981 (snippet): the last syllable always carries 'ein gut wahrnehmbarer fallender pitch'.
new_statements.exceptions: Unstressable (pre-stressing) elements: Persian enclitics -i (izafat), -i (indefinite article / relative linker); imperative person suffixes other than 2sg (a'l-din, a'l-dum vs. perfect al-du'm; Doerfer 1972: 299); 1pl aorist person marker (hat-i'miz 'we throw' vs. possessive hatimi'z 'our horse'); negative -mA (a'l-ma); copula/'esse' suffixes (xala'c-am) also in certain tenses; present-tense predicate suffixes; verbal suffix -; locative -ča (há'vča vs. ablative havdá', Doerfer 1978: 23). Lexical: some Persian loans (ba'li 'yes'). Vocative: initial stress (bu'zak!). Emphasis: accent shift or level stress (qani' vs. qa'ni). Items b)-d) of Doerfer's exception list were not recoverable from snippets.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated for citation/inflected word forms of the Xarrab (Kharrab) dialect, said by Doerfer to hold for the other Khalaj dialects; accent in word groups/phrases is treated separately (Doerfer 1988 par. 3.4 (5); Doerfer 1981). Doerfer marks accent with a following raised stroke in transcription.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand statements are Gerhard Doerfer's, based chiefly on the Xarrāb (Kharrab) dialect of Khalajistan (Markazi province, Iran); Doerfer 1988 states the accent rules 'ermittelt aus dem Dialekt von Xar[rab]' hold for the other Khalaj dialects too; Doerfer 1972 adds accent-marked forms from Talkhāb and Mowjān. Same language as Glottolog turk1303 (no sub-dialect glottocodes). Not to be confused with the Iranian-speaking 'Khalaj' mentioned by Ščerbak.

new_statements.translation: The accent rests as a norm on the last syllable of the word. (2) Exceptions are: a) some Persian words like bä'lī 'yes'; unstressed are the Persian suffixes -i (izafat) and -ī (indefinite article ...); ... imperative suffixes (a'l-dum 'I want to take' : al-du'm 'I took'); f) aorist 1st person plural (hat-i'miz 'we throw' : hatimi'z 'our horse'); g) the negative suffix (a'l-ma 'do not take!'); h) copula suffixes (xala'č+am 'I am a Khalaj' ...); i) predicate suffixes in the present; j) the verbal suffix -in. ... (4) The vocative shifts the accent to the first syllable (būzä'k 'the ice', but bū'zäk 'Ice!').

new_statements.reading: Khalaj has fixed word-final (last-syllable) stress of the common Turkic type, with a closed list of pre-stressing/unstressed suffixes (imperative, 1pl aorist, negative -ma, copular/predicate suffixes, verbal -in, Persian izafat and indefinite -ī), a few Persian loans with non-final stress, emphasis by accent shift, and vocative retraction to the first syllable. Doerfer 1981 adds that a falling pitch always sits on the last syllable whichever syllable is stressed, and that phrase-level main/secondary stress is fixed by the grammatical relation of the words. Coding suggestion for a new catalog record: fixed final stress (Turkic type), morphologically conditioned exceptions. Caveat: the 1988 and 1981 texts were read only as verbatim Google Books full-text snippets (no page images obtainable by automated download); the fully open corroboration actually read in full is Doerfer 1978 p. 23 ('Stress is just as in the other Turkic languages.. havda' "from the house" : ha'vča "in the house"').

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Zur Betonung ist zu sagen, dass alle Formen äusser der 2.Sg. unbetontes Suffix haben; im Dialekt von Talhäb z.B. heisst es al-и' 'nimm', aber ȧ'l-dīn 'nehmt', ȧ'l-lum 'ich möchte nehmen', al-duq 'lasst uns nehmen'; ... Durch den Akzent unterscheiden sich die Formen der 1. Person des Imperativs auch vom Perfekt: kö'r-düm 'ich will sehen': kör-dü'm 'ich sah'
sources.note: Morphological stress detail: all imperative forms except 2sg have an unstressed suffix (stem stress), so imperative 1sg kö'r-düm 'I want to see' contrasts with perfect kör-dü'm 'I saw' (suffix-final stress); presupposes that ordinary inflected words are stressed on the last syllable. Translation: 'On stress it must be said that all forms except the 2sg have an unstressed suffix; in the Talxab dialect e.g. al-i' "take", but a'l-dīn "take (pl.)", a'l-lum "I want to take".. By the accent the 1st-person imperative forms also differ from the perfect: kö'r-düm "I want to see" : kör-dü'm "I saw".'

sources.quote: Chaladsch: a. Gehörsmäßig liegt der Akzent auf der letzten Silbe. Wir wollen dies als die „normale Betonung" bezeichnen. Ausnahmen s. sub 3. b. Auf der letzten Silbe ruht stets ein gut wahrnehmbarer fallender pitch (Tonbewegung), gleichviel ob diese letzte Silbe (z.B. in qara 'schwarz') oder aber die erste (z.B. in ä'ngir 'gestern') betont ist. c. Die Länge der Silben richtet sich nach bekannten Mustern: Ceteris paribus sind Langvokale ... Die gehörsmäßige Empfindung des Akzents im Chaladsch ist weder gebunden an die Druckstärke, noch an die Tonhöhe ... Betonung: a) Iranische Wörter wie bä'li 'ja', xä'yli 'sehr' ...
